q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE British policy that contributed to the outbreak of rebellion in India in 1857.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the rebellion of 1857 spread beyond the sepoys to include broader Indian participation, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which British rule in India changed as a result of the rebellion of 1857.

sample_answers.a: The Doctrine of Lapse allowed the British to annex princely states whose rulers died without a natural heir, which dispossessed Indian nobles and created resentment among elites who lost their thrones and revenues.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, British land-revenue policies and annexations had alienated not only soldiers but also landlords, peasants, and deposed rulers, so when the sepoys mutinied, these groups saw an opportunity to join a wider revolt against British power.
sample_answers.c: After the rebellion, the British Crown took direct control of India from the East India Company (1858), and the British adopted a more cautious policy toward Indian princes and religious customs to avoid provoking another uprising.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the Indian rebellion of 1857 as the product of accumulating grievances rather than a single trigger. The greased cartridges — rumored to be coated with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindu and Muslim sepoys — were the spark, but the fuel had been gathering for decades. The East India Company's aggressive annexations under the Doctrine of Lapse dispossessed princes and nobles; new land-revenue settlements disrupted rural society and indebted peasants; and British social reforms and missionary activity convinced many Indians that the British intended to destroy their religions and traditions. When the sepoys at Meerut mutinied in May 1857, these wider resentments turned a military mutiny into a broad, if uncoordinated, rebellion against British rule.
—Historian's account of the Indian rebellion in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE group the proclamation calls upon to join the rebellion.
parts.b: Describe ONE grievance against the British stated in the proclamation.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why the proclamation emphasizes unity between Hindus and Muslims.

sample_answers.a: The proclamation calls upon the wealthy people of India — especially those connected to the Muslim royal families and regarded as the ‘pastors and masters of the people’ — to stake their lives and property in the struggle, framing the cause as one for all the Hindus and Mohammedans of Hindustan.
sample_answers.b: It charges that the people of Hindustan — both Hindus and Mohammedans — ‘are being ruined under the tyranny and oppression of the infidel and treacherous English,’ presenting British rule as unjust and destructive to all Indians.
sample_answers.c: The rebel leaders knew that Hindu-Muslim division would doom the uprising, so they stressed a common cause against the British; unity was essential because the rebels needed mass support to challenge British military power.

q2.stimulus:
It is well known to all that in this age the people of Hindustan, both Hindus and Mohammedans, are being ruined under the tyranny and oppression of the infidel and treacherous English. It is therefore the duty of all the wealthy people of India, especially those who have any sort of connection with any of the Mohammedan royal families and are considered the pastors and masters of the people, to stake their lives and property for the well-being of the public. With the blessings of God, and with the aid of the righteous, the English will be destroyed, and the people will be relieved of their sufferings.
—Adapted from the Azamgarh Proclamation, issued by the rebel government during the Indian rebellion, 1857

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the painting that reflects the British perspective on the rebellion of 1857.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the painting's depiction of the rebellion served British imperial interests after 1857.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Indian nationalists in the twentieth century reinterpreted the events of 1857 differently from the painting's portrayal.

sample_answers.a: The painting shows British soldiers and civilians as heroic defenders and the relief force as saviors, presenting the British as victims of treachery and the rebellion as a criminal mutiny rather than a legitimate uprising.
sample_answers.b: By celebrating British heroism and suffering at Lucknow, the painting justified harsh reprisals against the rebels and reinforced the narrative that British rule was a civilizing force besieged by barbarism, legitimizing continued imperial control.
sample_answers.c: Twentieth-century Indian nationalists reinterpreted 1857 as India's First War of Independence — a patriotic struggle for freedom — because they needed historical heroes and precedents for their own movement against British rule, directly challenging the British portrayal of the rebels as mere mutineers.

q3.stimulus: The image is Thomas Jones Barker's 1859 painting The Relief of Lucknow, 1857, depicting the moment British forces broke through to relieve the besieged British garrison at Lucknow during the Indian rebellion. The painting shows exhausted British defenders — soldiers, women, and children — greeting their rescuers, and became one of the most famous British images of the rebellion, widely reproduced as a symbol of imperial heroism.
